cards.front: What video streaming is mostly about
cards.back: Bandwidth, not storage. Shaped by network bandwidth, device variety and format variety.

cards.front: Concurrent streams for 500M viewers watching 30 minutes a day
cards.back: About 10 million at any moment on average, about 20 million at the evening peak.
About 26 Tb/s, 50+ Tb/s at peak. It has to come from thousands of caches near viewers.
Large files go straight to object storage, never through API servers, and a dropped connection resumes from the last part.
The control plane (API, playback, metadata) handles thousands of requests a second in the cloud; the data plane (segments) handles millions from ISP caches. They scale and fail separately.

cards.front: Why chunk a video before transcoding?
cards.back: Chunks cut at keyframes are transcoded in parallel by thousands of workers, so a video is playable in minutes and a failed chunk is simply retried.
Each video encoded at several renditions, e.g. 240p at 0.4 Mb/s up to 1080p at 5 Mb/s and 4K at 15 Mb/s; AV1 or VP9 save 30-50% over H.264.

cards.front: Why HLS and DASH replaced RTMP
cards.back: Both are plain HTTP: segments are ordinary files any HTTP cache can serve, with no long-lived streaming connections.
The player, per segment: throughput-based or buffer-based rules, starting low for a fast first frame.

cards.front: Push the head, pull the tail
cards.back: Popular titles are predicted and pushed into caches overnight; long-tail videos are pulled on a miss.

cards.front: Why steer via the playback service instead of DNS?
cards.back: It picks a specific cache using the viewer's network, cache health and load, returns fallbacks, and lets the player switch mid-stream.
Netflix's best single health signal; alert when it drops below the forecast for that time of day.

quiz.q: Viewers abandon because the first frame takes 5 seconds. Which player change helps most?
choices: Start at a low rendition and climb
quiz.why: Fast start at a low rendition shows the first frame quickly.

quiz.q: Transit costs explode as viewing grows. What is the main lever?
choices: More cache servers placed inside ISPs and at IXPs
quiz.why: The only affordable byte is one that never crosses the backbone.

quiz.q: A transcoding worker crashes and its chunk job is retried, and the upload-complete event is delivered twice. How do you avoid duplicate outputs?
choices: Lock the video row during processing
Run each video on one worker
Write every task's output to a deterministic path so retries overwrite
quiz.why: Idempotent tasks overwrite the same path instead of creating copies.

quiz.q: A viral video takes thousands of view increments a second on one database row. What is the fix?
choices: Count in memory or a stream job and write aggregated deltas
quiz.why: Aggregated deltas avoid the hot row; displayed counts lag by seconds.

quiz.q: The recommendations service is slow and the home page starts failing. What should happen?
choices: A circuit breaker trips and the page shows a cached or generic row
Route all traffic to one region
quiz.why: Each call has a timeout, retry budget and circuit breaker so the page degrades gracefully.

quiz.q: A big premiere is tomorrow evening. How do you avoid a cache stampede on the origin?
choices: Pull on first request as usual
Pre-position the title in every cache before release
quiz.why: Pushing ahead of demand means the premiere is served from caches.

quiz.q: The control plane in one region is struggling mid-evening. What must keep working?
choices: Playback already in progress, from caches with long-lived tokens
quiz.why: Stopping a film mid-scene is not acceptable; losing a row is.
